reasoning: A stronger payroll print raises the expected policy path, and the 5-year is the most policy-sensitive tenor; the record shows 27 of 33 up.
Hot jobs data reprices growth and the Fed path, lifting long yields too; the record shows 27 of 33 up.
A payroll miss pulls forward expected easing, so front-to-belly yields fall; the record shows 22 of 31 down.
A jobs beat widens the expected US rate differential and supports the dollar; the record shows 22 of 33 up.
A jobs miss lowers real yields and the dollar, the two main drivers of gold; the record shows 21 of 31 up.
Yen crosses are the purest expression of the US-Japan rate gap, which a jobs beat widens.
Weak consumer spending lowers the growth and policy outlook, pulling 5-year yields down; the record shows 26 of 36 down.
The mirror of the miss: a strong consumer pushes out easing and lifts policy-sensitive yields.
A retail miss lowers growth expectations and long yields with them; the record shows 25 of 36 down.
When breakevens have been rising, inflation is the market's focus and an upside CPI surprise feeds straight into the expected policy path.
An upside inflation print mechanically raises expected inflation priced in TIPS breakevens; the record shows 23 of 34 up.
A soft CPI print lowers priced inflation compensation; the record shows 28 of 51 down.
In an inflation-scare regime a soft print relieves the expected tightening path and front yields fall more reliably than in calm times.
When yields have risen fast the Fed is reacting to inflation, so a hot CPI means more tightening and equities sell off.
In a tightening scare a soft CPI print signals the peak in rates is near, which equities rally on.
When rates are already rising quickly, an inflation upside surprise raises policy uncertainty and implied volatility.
Long-duration growth stocks are the most rate-sensitive, so a soft print during a rate scare lifts the Nasdaq most.
When the Fed is in reaction mode, hot inflation widens the expected rate differential and lifts the dollar.
Event-risk premium built into implied volatility before a decision is released once a hold passes; the record shows 75 of 148 down.
The more fear has built in the month before the meeting, the more premium a non-event hold releases.
After a fear build-up a steady Fed removes a tail risk and equities get a relief bid; the record already shows holds lean up.
An in-line jobs report removes the event premium without changing the outlook; the record shows 44 of 78 down.
An announcement that tightens supply raises crude directly; the record shows 17 of 21 up.
Energy equities' earnings track crude, so a supply cut lifts the sector; the record shows 26 of 45 up.
Gasoline follows crude through refining margins, so a supply cut lifts it the same day; the record shows 13 of 20 up.
A decision that adds supply or fails to cut lowers crude; the record shows 11 of 13 down.
Energy is the swing component of headline inflation, so a crude supply shock lifts inflation breakevens; the record shows it up.
A cut after a slump is the cartel defending the price floor, more credible and less priced in than a cut in a firm market.
Gold is the classic geopolitical haven and the bid builds over the following week; the record shows 19 of 29 up.
Violent acts raise expected defence spending and orders, which lifts aerospace and defence shares over the week.
Gulf landfalls shut in offshore gas production and threaten LNG and processing capacity; the record shows 10 of 16 up.
Gulf Coast refining is concentrated in hurricane paths, so outages tighten gasoline supply over the week.
A miss cuts expected cash flows and the stock is repriced at once; the record shows 1387 of 2053 down and it holds walk-forward.
A beat raises expected cash flows; the record shows 4301 of 7651 up.
A stock that has run up into the report prices high expectations, so a miss disappoints a crowded long base and is punished harder.
A beaten-down stock carries low expectations and short interest, so a beat forces a relief rally and short covering.
After a strong run-up the market wants a beat; merely in-line results disappoint, and in-line already leans down in the record.
A sharp run into the print means positioning is long, and the unwinding of that position after a miss continues through the week.
The same expectations effect for the other report set: a miss after a strong run-up meets the highest bar and falls furthest.
A split announced on its own signals management confidence and widens retail access; the record shows 30 of 45 up.
